newsitem.title: USA: Espy probe reaches into Clinton inner circle.
newsitem.headline: Espy probe reaches into Clinton inner circle.

text.p: The criminal investigation of former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy has reached into President Bill Clinton's inner circle with a recent grand jury appearance by one of the president's closest confidants, sources familiar with the investigation said.

Vernon Jordan, a longtime close presidential friend, was summoned last month by independent counsel Don Smaltz to answer questions before a grand jury about his role as head of Clinton's transition team after the 1992 election and how Espy was chosen as secretary of agriculture.
But his court appearance raised eyebrows in Washington where there has long been speculation that the lengthy, but so far low profile investigation, could spell trouble for the White House.

"I wouldn't be surprised if Smaltz is following leads and would not be adverse to making charges even on the presidential level if that's where his leads take him. You can become quite a historical figure that way," said Georgetown University law professor Paul Rothstein.
Rothstein and others stressed that just being called before a grand jury did not implicate anyone, and said it would be better not to read too much in the Jordan appearance.

Nevertheless, an investigation that began with a relatively narrowly defined focus of impropriety by a former Cabinet member appeared to have broadened to include influence-peddling and political deal-making in Washington by others.
"The relationship between business and the government or administration officials, in the context of gratuities of Espy, is being investigated," said an official in Smaltz's office.
Espy has been under investigation since late 1994 for allegedly accepting illegal gifts and favors while he was agriculture secretary from companies his agency regulated.

The original allegations against Espy, a former congressman from Mississippi, stemmed from gifts he took from Arkansas-based Tyson Foods Inc, the nation's biggest poultry processor whose chairman Don Tyson has long enjoyed close ties with Clinton, former governor of Arkansas.
The Tyson Foods-Espy connection has been a central focus of the investigation, and speculation is growing that indictments will be issued later this year.

While Smaltz has been accused by some of overstepping his original authority, his methodical investigation resulted in criminal indictments and charges against more than a dozen individuals and concerns, including the Washington lobbyist for Tyson.
It also resulted in guilty verdicts or fines against the largest fruit cooperative and the second-biggest crop insurance company in the country.

While Smaltz's office denied the special prosecutor was investigating any connections between the Espy affair and campaign contributions to the Democratic party, some sources familiar with the investigation said it could indeed lead to White House officials if necessary.

Republicans in Congress planned major hearings on contributions to the Democrats during the election campaign last year by foreign citizens, and questionable White House dealings with leading business figures.
In the meantime Smaltz summoned some high-profile witnesses before the grand jury.

Besides Jordan, television journalist Mike Wallace appeared this week in court answering questions related to an expose he did in 1994 on CBS News "60 Minutes" on Don Tyson and his relationship with Clinton. Former Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who was also a key player in the 1992 transition team, may also be questioned by the grand jury, sources said.
